context:
Overall review topic: the impact of large language models (ChatGPT-style chatbots, AI answer engines such as Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, and AI shopping assistants such as Amazon Rufus) on CONSUMER SEARCH — how people look for products, services, prices and information before buying — and research on how to better design or use LLMs for consumer search. The review spans economics, marketing, and computer science (IR, recommender systems, HCI). Seven parallel streams cover: (01) economic theory of search costs and market outcomes, (02) empirical evidence on how consumers use LLM search, (03) effects on search engines, publishers, advertising and generative engine optimization, (04) marketing: brand visibility, bias and manipulation of LLM product recommendations, (05) LLM agents as delegated shoppers, (06) CS/IR system design for LLM-based product search, (07) HCI: trust, over-reliance and interface design. Stay inside YOUR stream; mention cross-stream papers briefly only.

Prior reviews by the same user already cover (do NOT re-review in depth, cite only if directly relevant): (a) LLM conversational recommender systems (ReDial benchmark issues, LLM vs classic recommenders, simulated-user evaluation); (b) cost-aware sequential search in LLMs (whether LLM agents trade off search value vs cost, Bayesian-optimal stopping; key papers include 'Shopping by algorithm: How agentic AI deploys human heuristics as a surrogate consumer' and 'Calibrate-Then-Act').

Today is 2026-11-03: include 2025-2026 preprints (arXiv, SSRN, NBER) as well as peer-reviewed work. SSRN and NBER are key for economics and marketing working papers.

streams.title: How LLMs change search costs and market outcomes: economic theory and evidence
streams.question: What does economics (theory and empirics) say about how LLMs and AI assistants change consumer search costs, and the downstream effects on price dispersion, competition, market concentration, product variety, and consumer welfare? Include search-cost models (sequential/ordered search, Diamond paradox), delegated search to AI intermediaries, 'algorithmic consumers', steering/self-preferencing by AI intermediaries, and policy/antitrust analysis of AI assistants as gatekeepers.

streams.title: How consumers actually search with LLMs: experiments and field evidence
streams.question: What empirical evidence (lab experiments, randomized field experiments, surveys, clickstream/log data) exists on how consumers use LLM-based search (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Bing Chat, AI Overviews, shopping assistants) versus traditional search engines — in terms of search effort, time, number of queries, breadth of options considered, decision quality, purchase outcomes, and satisfaction? Include adoption and substitution patterns (e.g., ChatGPT reducing Google usage) and heterogeneity across consumers.

streams.title: Effects on search engines, publishers, ads and generative engine optimization
streams.question: How do LLM answer engines (Google AI Overviews, Bing Copilot, Perplexity, ChatGPT search) affect the search ecosystem: click-through and traffic to websites and publishers ('zero-click'), search advertising markets and ad placement in LLM answers, and the rise of generative engine optimization (GEO) — how sellers and content creators try to get cited or recommended by LLMs? Include economics of content provision, ad auctions for LLM outputs, and measurement studies.

streams.title: Brand visibility, bias and manipulation in LLM product recommendations
streams.question: What does marketing and CS research find about which brands and products LLMs recommend to consumers: brand bias and popularity/incumbent bias, consistency of recommendations, sensitivity to prompt wording and consumer persona, vulnerability to manipulation (strategic text, prompt injection on product pages, fake reviews), sponsored or persuasive content in LLM answers, and implications for brand strategy and consumer trust?

streams.title: LLM agents as shoppers: rationality, biases and agent markets
streams.question: How well do LLM agents perform as delegated shoppers on behalf of consumers (agentic commerce)? Cover choice rationality and consistency (e.g., GARP tests, revealed preference), behavioral biases (position, anchoring, decoy effects), benchmarks for shopping agents (WebShop, ShoppingBench and successors), alignment of agent choices with the user's true preferences, and market-level effects when sellers and buyers both use AI agents (agent-to-agent negotiation, simulated marketplaces).
streams.extra: The prior cost-aware search review covered cost-sensitivity of LLM stopping; focus here on choice quality, biases, preference alignment and multi-agent markets.

streams.title: Designing LLM systems for product and consumer search
streams.question: What CS/IR research shows how to better design LLM-based systems for consumer and product search: conversational product search, clarifying questions and preference elicitation, retrieval-augmented generation over catalogs and reviews, LLM query understanding and rewriting in e-commerce, generative retrieval, product QA, comparison/summarization of options, and evaluation methods (offline metrics, simulated users, online A/B tests at companies like Amazon, Alibaba, Walmart, Instacart)? Which design choices have demonstrated gains and of what size?
streams.extra: The prior CRS review covered conversational recommendation benchmarks (ReDial) and LLM-vs-classic recommender comparisons. Focus here on search/QA/elicitation design and deployed e-commerce systems.

streams.title: Trust, over-reliance and interface design for LLM consumer search
streams.question: What HCI and behavioral research finds about user trust and over-reliance on LLM search answers in consumer decisions: effects of hallucinations and errors, source citations, uncertainty or confidence displays, answer-vs-link presentation, persuasion and sycophancy, effects on learning and exploration (narrowing of considered options), and which interface interventions improve decision quality?
